steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The colour wheel organises hues: primary (red, yellow, blue), secondary (orange, green, purple), tertiary (red-orange, blue-green etc).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Complementary colours sit opposite on the wheel and create maximum contrast and visual vibration when placed together.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Colour has emotional and psychological impact — warm colours (reds, oranges) feel energetic; cool colours (blues, greens) feel calm.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Tints (add white), shades (add black) and tones (add grey) expand your palette beyond pure hues.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Create a series of experimental studies exploring colour theory and mixing. Annotate your process. | Research an artist or designer who works with colour theory and mixing. Write a critical analysis of their approach and explain how it has informed your own work. | Evaluate the effectiveness of your experiments with colour theory and mixing. Which approaches were most successful and why?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A range of experimental studies showing different approaches to colour theory and mixing, each annotated with media, technique and purpose. Show development from initial experiments to refined outcome | A critical analysis naming a specific artist/designer, using specialist vocabulary, explaining their context and approach, and making clear connections to personal work. | A reflective evaluation identifying successful and less successful experiments, explaining WHY using technical and conceptual language, and showing how evaluation led to further refinement.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Address ALL four Assessment Objectives — AO1 (develop), AO2 (refine), AO3 (record), AO4 (present) Show the FULL creative journey — from initial research to final outcome Annotate your work using specialist vocabulary (not just "I like it") Draw from primary sources wherever possible — real objects, not photos Experiment with a RANGE of media and techniques before selecting Make clear connections between artist research and your own developing work
